We are going to do something different in this episode. We are so far asking questions in Gemini CLI, using the built-in commands, consuming Model Context Protocol (MCP) Servers and in the last episode, we took a look at custom slash commands. This episode is all about becoming a creator of a different sort. We will be writing our own MCP Servers that we can consume in Gemini CLI. While we will see some the mechanics of bundling functionality into MCP Servers, the goal will be to give you the tools and the foundation to build some real world MCP Servers that you could then even distribute to others to use.

This episode will require that you are familiar with Python. We will a bit of Python development, starting servers and more, to build out the MCP Server. Even if Python is not your preferred language, the episode should give you the mechanics to seek out the required packages / frameworks for [writing MCP Servers in a language of your choice](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol).

By writing your own MCP Server, you will be giving Gemini CLI new skills that are private to you, connecting it to our proprietary data, and enforcing your unique workflows.

Here is the flow for this episode:

1. We will be setting up the Python development environment and then using [**FastMCP**](https://gofastmcp.com/getting-started/welcome), a simple and powerful Python framework that makes building these servers a breeze.
2. We will start off with a simple “Hello, World!” MCP server and connect it locally to Gemini CLI.
3. Design and construct a sophisticated, real-world “Technical Editor” agent with custom tools and prompts.

In addition to the above, we will also highlight resources that help you deploy these MCP Server resources to Google Cloud in a secure fashion, which you can then call from Gemini CLI.

Let’s go.

## Before we start: Update your Gemini CLI version

If it’s been a while that you used Gemini CLI, make sure that you are running the latest version of the tool. Here’s a handy command to upgrade your Gemini CLI to the latest version.

`npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@latest`

Do a `gemini -v`command and ensure that you are seeing atleast `0.4.0` or above.

## Prerequisites and Setup

Open your terminal and run these commands to create a directory in which we will be doing most of the development work. You can create a directory name of your choice, but I have used `my-mcp-server` over here. Please open your terminal and follow along.

```
mkdir my-mcp-server
cd my-mcp-server
```

Let’s get our digital workbench ready.

1. **Python &**`uv`: Our server will be written in Python. You'll need Python 3.10 or newer. We'll also use `uv`, an extremely fast Python package installer and project manager that will simplify our dependency management. If you don't have `uv`, you can install it easily by following the [official instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

**(Optional) Google Cloud SDK**: We will not be deploying our MCP server to Google Cloud but will point you to excellent resources that makes this possible. So in case you wish to do that, you will need to have the `gcloud` command-line tool installed and authenticated, along with a Google Cloud Project.

## Installing FastMCP

Once you have Python and uv in place, its time to install [FastMCP](https://gofastmcp.com/getting-started/welcome). This framework abstracts away all the low-level complexities of the MCP specification. Instead of wrestling with JSON-RPC protocols and schema definitions, we get to write simple, clean Python functions.

Let’s create the Python environment first via `uv venv`. Activate it via the `source .venv/bin/activate` command.

Then let’s install FastMCP: `uv pip install fastmcp`

You should see output indicating that FastMCP and its dependencies have been successfully installed.

## Our First MCP Server

Let’s build our first, minimal MCP server now. We will stick to tradition and build the “Hello, World!” of MCP Servers.

### The “Hello, World!” of MCP

Create a new file in your project directory named `server.py` and add the following code.

```
from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP(name="MyFirstMCPServer")

@mcp.tool
def greet(name:str) -> str:
    """Returns a friendly greeting"""
    return f"Hello {name}! Its a pleasure to connect from your first MCP Server."

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="http", port="8080")
```

Let’s break down this code, piece by piece:

- `mcp = FastMCP(name="...")`: This line creates an instance of the FastMCP server. We give it a human-readable name that will appear in the Gemini CLI.
- `@mcp.tool`: This Python decorator instantly transforms the `greet` function into a full-fledged tool that Gemini can discover and use. FastMCP intelligently uses the function's name (`greet`) as the tool's name, the docstring (`"""..."""`) as its description, and the Python type hints (`name: str`, `-> str`) to automatically generate the data schema that the MCP protocol requires.
- While FastMCP supports [multiple transport options](https://gofastmcp.com/deployment/running-server#transport-options) available in MCP, we shall we using the [Streamable HTTP](https://gofastmcp.com/deployment/running-server#streamable-http) option, which helps to expose your MCP server via HTTP. It is the recommended transport for web-based deployments. To run a server using Streamable HTTP, you can use the `run()` method with the `transport` argument set to `"http"`. This will start a Uvicorn server on the default host (`127.0.0.1`) and with the port number that we have specified i.e. `8080`.

### Running the MCP Server Locally

In your terminal, you can simply run the `server.py` file via Python or you can use the `fastmcp` tool also to run the server.

The `fastmcp` tool allows us to do multiple things and if you just run the command `fastmcp` without any parameters, you will see the various options as shown below:

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*Klu8ZJZ6EJ-ivKgYT4Z8sg.png)

Let’s use that since we will also be using it in dev mode to test it out with the MCP Inspector.

If you run it via the `fastmcp` tool then, you need to read this note, that I have taken from the documentation:

> When using `fastmcp run`, it ignores the `if __name__ == "__main__"` block entirely. Instead, it looks for a FastMCP object named `mcp`, `server`, or `app` and calls its `run()` method directly with the transport options you specify.This means you can use `fastmcp run` to override the transport specified in your code, which is particularly useful for testing or changing deployment methods without modifying the code.

So, let’s start up our MCP Server via the command shown below:

```
fastmcp run server.py --transport="http" --port="8080"
```

You should see an output similar to the one shown below:

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*HMCybAmOUuFI1YTlUMj5lQ.png)

Note that the MCP Server URL is shown as `http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp/` [.](http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp/)

### Testing our server via MCP Inspector

Let’s first use the MCP Inspector tool to validate if our MCP Server is working fine. Currently, we have just one tool ( `greet`) but make it a practice to test things out first.

The MCP Inspector is a tool that lets us test out the MCP Server interactively. It allows you to check out the tools, prompts and resources that a MCP Server provides to the outside world.

In another terminal window, launch the inspector via the `fastmcp` command as shown below:

`fastmcp dev server.py --ui-port="9080" --server-port="5080"`

We are providing a UI port since the MCP Inspector is a web application that provides a user interface to connect to and test out MCP Servers. It also uses a Proxy server port to tunnel requests in and from the MCP Server.

## Connecting Gemini CLI to our MCP Server

How do we tell Gemini CLI about our new local MCP server? If you have been following the tutorial series so far, this should be familiar ground when we configured some [external MCP Servers in Part 5](https://medium.com/google-cloud/gemini-cli-tutorial-series-part-5-github-mcp-server-b557ae449e6e).

To refresh, we need to edit the global Gemini CLI settings file, which is located at `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Open this file in your favorite editor.

Add the following `mcpServers` configuration. If you already have an `mcpServers` block, just add `"myLocalServer"` to it.

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-mcp-server": {
      "httpUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp/"
    }
  }
}
```

This configuration tells Gemini CLI everything it needs to know to connect to our MCP server.

### Verification

Save your `settings.json` file and launch Gemini CLI in your terminal:

Once the CLI is running, type the `/mcp` command and press Enter. This command lists all configured MCP servers and their available tools. You should see our new server listed!

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Seeing `my-mcp-server` and the `greet` tool means everything is working perfectly. Now for the final test. Give Gemini a prompt that encourages it to use your new tool:

`greet Romin Irani`

Gemini will recognize that this requires an external tool and will ask for your permission.

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*2dJTr7RuuAEReskdxTYbzQ.png)

```

```

Congratulations! You have successfully built and integrated your first custom MCP server.

## The Automated Technical Editor

Now that we understand the basic workflow, let’s build something useful. We’re going to create an AI agent that acts as a technical editor, capable of analyzing a piece of text against a set of stylistic and readability rules. This is a powerful, real-world use case for custom AI agents.

### Distinguishing Tools from Prompts

Before we write more code, it’s essential to understand **Tools** and **Prompts** and the support that **FastMCP** has for them.

**What is a Tool?**

Think of a **Tool** as the agent’s _hands_. It’s a discrete, deterministic function that performs a specific action. In FastMCP, you create a tool by simply decorating a regular Python function with `@mcp.tool`.

This function takes structured input (like text or numbers) and returns a structured output. Examples include calculating a value, querying a database, calling an external API, or reading a file.

The beauty of FastMCP is that it automatically exposes your Python function—its name, its descriptive docstring, and its typed parameters—as a capability that Gemini can understand and use without any complex configuration. It's the fundamental building block for giving your AI new, concrete skills.

**What is a Prompt?**

If a Tool is the agent’s hands, then a **Prompt** is its _brain_. It’s not just a simple string of text; it’s a template for a conversation that defines a high-level task or workflow. You create one by decorating a function with `@mcp.prompt`.

The purpose of a prompt is to _plan and orchestrate_ the use of available tools to achieve a complex goal. For example, a prompt might instruct the AI to first use a `read_file` tool, then a `summarize_text` tool, and finally a `format_report` tool.

In the Gemini CLI, these MCP prompts often **become powerful, custom slash commands** that you can invoke directly from your terminal.

The real magic happens when a prompt’s instructions tell the LLM to use the available tools. For our technical editor, we will create a master `/tech-edit` command. This command will be an MCP _prompt_ that orchestrates the use of several custom _tools_ to produce a comprehensive report.

### Building the Technical Editor’s Tools

Let’s equip our editor with some capabilities (2 new tools and one prompt). Specifically pay attention to the prompt `/tech-edit` . It will instruct Gemini on how to behave and how to use the tools we just created. Notice how the prompt acts as a set of instructions. It explicitly tells Gemini to call `calculate_readability` and `check_for_weasel_words`, and then to combine those results with its own powerful language analysis capabilities.

## Deploying to Cloud Run

So far we have been running the MCP Server locally. This is important so that we can test it out locally and once you are ready to share this with others, you can opt to securely host this in the Cloud.

Google Cloud Run provides a solid platform to deploy your MCP Server. I do not want to reinvent the whole discussion here on how you can do that since there is an excellent codelab “ [How to deploy a secure MCP Server to Cloud Run](https://codelabs.developers.google.com/codelabs/cloud-run/how-to-deploy-a-secure-mcp-server-on-cloud-run#0)” authored by

We’ve covered writing our own MCP Server and then provided a real world example of combining both a prompt and a couple of tools to achieve a custom command in Gemini CLI.

web.title: Set up Gemini CLI with Remote MCP - Atlan Documentation
web.description: Learn how to configure Gemini CLI to use Atlan's Remote MCP server for seamless AI-powered metadata access.
web.markdown:
[Skip to main content](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp#__docusaurus_skipToContent_fallback)

On this page

You can connect Gemini CLI to the Atlan Remote MCP server. This lets you search for assets, explore lineage, update metadata, create glossary terms, and more directly from your command line.

## Prerequisites [​](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp\#prerequisites "Direct link to Prerequisites")

Before you begin, make sure you have:

- An Atlan tenant with **Remote MCP** enabled.
- [Node.js 18](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v18.18.0) or newer installed on your system.

## Install Gemini CLI [​](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp\#install-gemini-cli "Direct link to Install Gemini CLI")

You can follow these steps to install Gemini CLI on Windows, macOS, or Linux. The installation commands are the same across all operating systems.

1. Open your terminal application. Terminal on macOS, Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows, or any terminal emulator on Linux.

2. Run the following command to install Gemini CLI globally:





```bash
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
```









If you prefer not to install globally, you can run Gemini CLI directly using:





```text
npx @google/gemini-cli
```

3. Verify the installation by running:





```bash
gemini --version
```


## Set up Gemini CLI configuration Recommended models: Gemini 2.5/3.0 [​](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp\#set-up-gemini-cli-configuration- "Direct link to set-up-gemini-cli-configuration-")

After installing Gemini CLI, follow these steps to authenticate and set up your configuration file.

1. In your terminal, start Gemini CLI by running:





```bash
gemini
```









Sign in using Google login or a [Gemini API key](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/api-key). After authentication, your credentials are stored locally.

2. In your terminal, locate the Gemini settings file, which is stored at:





```bash
~/.gemini/settings.json
```

3. If the file or folder doesn't exist, create them by running:





```bash
mkdir -p ~/.gemini
touch ~/.gemini/settings.json
```

4. Use this file for all future MCP configuration. Any settings you add for the Atlan Remote MCP server must be added to `settings.json`.


## Set up Remote MCP [​](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp\#set-up-remote-mcp "Direct link to Set up Remote MCP")

You can connect Gemini CLI to the Atlan Remote MCP server using either OAuth or an API key. Choose the method that best fits your use case.

- OAuth
- API Key

You can set up OAuth if you want Gemini CLI to connect using your Atlan login and permissions.

1. In your terminal, open the Gemini configuration file located at:





```bash
~/.gemini/settings.json
```









Add (or merge) the following section into the file:





```json
{
     "mcpServers": {
       "Atlan OAuth Server": {
         "httpUrl": "https://<your-tenant>.atlan.com/mcp",
         "oauth": {
           "enabled": true
         }
       }
     }
}
```









Replace `<your-tenant>` with your Atlan tenant subdomain. For example, if your Atlan URL is `riotgames.atlan.com`, use `https://riotgames.atlan.com/mcp`.

This shouldn't include headers or tokens. Gemini CLI handles the entire OAuth flow.

2. Save the file and restart Gemini CLI:





```bash
gemini
```









After restart, the OAuth server becomes visible but won't be authorized yet.

3. In your active Gemini session, check for servers that require authentication by running:





```bash
/mcp auth
```









You see output similar to:





```text
Servers requiring authentication:
     Atlan OAuth Server (NOT AUTHENTICATED)
```

4. In the same session, authenticate the Atlan OAuth server by running:





```bash
/mcp auth Atlan OAuth Server
```









A browser window opens, you sign in, and Gemini stores the OAuth tokens locally. Once complete, the server becomes fully functional.

If tokens expire later, simply run the same command again.

5. After completing authentication, verify that the server is connected and begin using Atlan MCP tools.

In your active Gemini session, run:





```text
/mcp
```









You see output similar to:





```text
Atlan API Key Server (CONNECTED)
Atlan OAuth Server (CONNECTED)
```









For more information, see the list of [Atlan MCP tools](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/atlan-mcp-overview#atlan-mcp-tools).


You can set up API Key authentication if you want Gemini CLI to connect using a static token for automation or service-to-service use cases.

1. In Atlan, generate an API key by going to **Admin Settings → API Keys / Tokens**.

2. In your terminal, open the Gemini configuration file located at:





```bash
~/.gemini/settings.json
```









Add (or merge) the following section into the file:





```json
{
     "mcpServers": {
       "Atlan API Key Server": {
         "httpUrl": "https://<your-tenant>.atlan.com/mcp/api-key",
         "headers": {
           "Authorization": "Bearer <atlan_api_key_here>"
         }
       }
     }
}
```









Replace:
   - `<your-tenant>` with your Atlan tenant subdomain (for example, if your Atlan URL is `riotgames.atlan.com`, use `https://riotgames.atlan.com/mcp/api-key`)
   - `<atlan_api_key_here>` with your real Atlan API key or token
3. Save the file and restart Gemini CLI:





```bash
gemini
```









Because this server uses static headers, it usually begins working immediately if the token is valid.

4. After completing authentication, verify that the server is connected and begin using Atlan MCP tools.

In your active Gemini session, run:





```text
/mcp
```









You see output similar to:





```text
Atlan API Key Server (CONNECTED)
Atlan OAuth Server (CONNECTED)
```









For more information, see the list of [Atlan MCP tools](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/atlan-mcp-overview#atlan-mcp-tools).


## Need help? [​](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp\#need-help "Direct link to Need help?")

If you have any issues while configuring the integration, contact [**Atlan Support**](https://docs.atlan.com/support/submit-request) for assistance.

- [Set up Gemini CLI configuration](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp#set-up-gemini-cli-configuration-)
- [Set up Remote MCP](https://docs.atlan.com/product/capabilities/atlan-ai/how-tos/gemini-remote-mcp#set-up-remote-mcp)

In this Gemini CLI Crash Course series, I'll show you how to get up an running wth the CLI in a project, use extensions & MCP servers, add an API key to access Gemini 3 models and more.

🔗👇 Context7

```

## Transcript

All right. So, we've seen now a lot of the core functionality of the Gemini CLI and we've used that to interact with our codebase locally on this computer. But what if we want Gemini to interact with services or APIs outside of our local project? For example, our application might use a backend service like Superbase or Firebase or something else and we might want Gemini to interact with that service as part of implementing a new feature like setting up a new data model or adding authentication or something. Well, by default, coding agents like Gemini or Cloud Code can't really do that, but we can use something called an MCP server to extend Gemini's capabilities to interact with those external services and APIs. Now, this is not going to be a deep dive into the architecture of MCP servers and how they work under the hood, but I do want to give you a brief overview so that you know what's going on from kind of a bird's eye perspective. So MCP stands for model context protocol and it's a protocol that was put into place by anthropic who created claude code and other cla models and they made this protocol as a way for AI clients like the Gemini CLI and therefore the AI model itself to interact with external services and data sources. So let's say for example we have a Firebase backend right and we want Gemini to interact with that backend service to help build out the application. Well, to do that, we can add the Firebase MCP server to the Gemini CLI. And when we do that, the MCP server exposes a bunch of extra tools that Gemini can trigger and tell the MCP server to run them. Now, those tools defined in the MCP server and exposed to the Gemini CLI are basically just functions that when triggered, run some code and send requests to the Firebase service. It then takes the response and hands that back to Gemini. For example, the Firebase MCP server exposes a tool called Firebase list projects which reaches out to Firebase and returns all the projects that you have for your account. So if we ask the Gemini CLI to do something which requires it to know about our Firebase projects, then it can trigger this tool to reach out to Firebase, grab our projects and return them to the Gemini CLI. And then in turn the AI model can decide what to do next based on that response. And the important thing to understand is that it's not the AI model itself reaching out to those external services. It doesn't know how to interact with them. It only knows the tools provided as context by the MCP server that we add and then it can request those tools to be run by the MCP server. Now, this is an oversimplification, but it's enough of a mental model to get started. But anyway, let's try adding an MCP server to the Gemini CLI. Now, in this lesson, we're going to be adding the official MCP server for a service called Context 7, which is a huge collection of the most recent and up-to-date docs of loads of frameworks and libraries like Next, N, React, View, Tailwind, you name it. And the MCP server for this exposes tools to get and search those docs for whatever framework we're interested in. And this is good because if we're implementing a new framework or new feature from a framework, then we can tell Gemini to use the context 7 MCP server to find out the latest official guidance on how to implement it. Because without doing so, then the AI model could occasionally use old and sometimes outdated approaches based on the training data it's been fed and its cutff point. So by using something like context 7 in our development workflow with a code engag agent we can be more confident I guess in the code it produces being uptodate and correct. Now to use the context 7 MCP server you'll need to sign up for a free account at context7.com and then generate free API key and you can do that by coming to your dashboard and then scrolling down until you see the create API key button. So just click on that, give your key a name, and then copy the key once it's been generated because you'll be needing that later on. In fact, you might want to paste it in notepad or something else for now because we'll be copying another snippet of code in a moment as well. So we have the API key and next we need to add the context 7 MCP server to the Gemini CLI to use it. to see how to do that. We can head to the Context 7 install guide by clicking on this link up here, which opens the GitHub repo for the MCP server. Now, if we scroll down the page a bit, we're going to see options for different clients like cursor, clawed code, client, etc. And if you keep on scrolling, you will eventually come to the Gemini CLI option, which we need to expand. And when we do that, we're going to see a snippet of code that we need to copy. Now, there's actually two options here, adding a remote server or a local one. and where possible I use the remote option. So I'm going to highlight all of this bit of code here except the surrounding curly braces and copy that. Okay, so back in VS Code then we need to register this MCP server so that Gemini knows about it. And to do that we can open the settings.json file and just add it right here. So inside this settings object, I'm going to paste in the snippet of code I copied from the context 7 docs. And this registers this context 7 MCP server for this project. And any other MCP servers we add to this project would be configured like this inside the same MCP servers property. And again those MCP servers would be registered and available to only this project. Now you can add MCP servers globally to the Gemini CLI and you would do that in the global settings file using the same MCP servers property like this. But for this series, we're going to be adding this MCP server to just this project. Anyway, if you take a look at this server configuration, you can see that we've got the URL to reach the server and then down here, we've got some headers and we need to supply an API key right here, which is what we got before from the context 7 website. Now, instead of adding the API key here directly where it might accidentally get pushed to a public repo, we can keep it inside av file instead. And then Gemini CLI allows us to reference those variables inside this settings file. So let's start by making av file first in the root of the project. And then inside this file, I'm going to make a new environment variable called context 7 all caps and then underscore API key. And then we need to set that equal to the API key we got from the context 7 website which I'm going to copy from my other screen right now so that I can paste it back in over here. So now let's save this file and head back to the settings.json file where we can reference this variable. And we can do that by coming to this value right here and then replacing it with dollar sign curly braces and then inside that the name of the variable which was all uppercase context 7 API key and importantly this stays inside the double quotes. So then now we've added the server we can start using it by coming to the Gemini CLI and first of all quitting the current session by using the quit command. Then we can start a new one by typing Gemini in the terminal and hitting enter. And I'm doing this because a lot of the time when you add a new server or new configuration, Gemini doesn't always pick up on that until you start another session. Anyway, now we've done that, we can run the MCP command to verify the MCP server was added because this command lists all the MCP servers it finds for the project. And you can see that now we have this context 7 server which comes with a couple of tools to get a library ID and then to actually get the docs for a library. Now when we're chatting with Gemini, if we want to check context 7 for any docs, we don't have to explicitly tell it to use any specific tools because these tools provide enough context to the model so that it automatically knows which ones to call when it needs to. So I could just use a prompt like this which I'm going to paste in and that says use context 7 to check I've set up vest correctly for a nux app in the vest config file. All right. Then I'm going to manually add that config file by typing the at symbol and searching for vest and then selecting it. And if I hit enter, we should see that at some point the Gemini CL asks us for permission to run a tool from the context 7 MCP server. And there it is. Allow execution of MCP tool resolve library ID from server context 7. So I'm just going to say yes. And I'll say always allow this tool and press enter. And then now it wants to run the other tool get library docs. So again I'm going to say yes and always allow that tool. Okay. So now it's done and it says yes your vestconfig.ts is correctly set up for a Nux application. It verified this against the official Nux testing documentation and checked the project structure. All right, cool. So that's all done now. And again, anytime I wanted to check the docs for something or I wanted Gemini to check the docs for something before it implements a feature, I can just ask it to use context 7. Okay, so that's how we add an MCP server. And in the case of this context 7 one, something I normally do is add an instruction to my Gemini file telling Gemini to use the docs from context 7 whenever it adds a new framework specific feature. And that way I don't have to manually ask it to do that every time I'm sending a prompt. Now sometimes it might skip that step and in which case you can manually tell it to do so, but generally it follows those instructions. All right, so we've seen now how to use MCP servers with the Gemini CLI. And next I want to show you how Gemini CLI extensions work. So I'm on the Gemini CLI website and up here you can see a link to the extensions page. And when we click on that we're going to see a list of all the extensions available to us that we can install. Now these extensions are something unique to the Gemini CLI and they're basically small packages which can include MCP server configurations like we just saw a context normally in the form of markdown files and custom commands. And sometimes an extension can be just one of these things and sometimes it can be a combination of all of them. It depends on the extension. # How to Add MCP Servers to Gemini CLI (Step-by-Step)

Set up MCP servers in Gemini CLI in 5 minutes. Covers settings.json config, BrainGrid MCP, Supabase, and troubleshooting common errors.

Vanshika Rana

January 26, 2026

12 min read

![How to Add MCP Servers to Gemini CLI (Step-by-Step)](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/headers/gemini-mcp.svg)

I've been using **Gemini CLI MCP servers** for a while now, and they've completely changed how I build with AI. Instead of copying schemas into every prompt and fixing placeholder code, Gemini connects directly to my databases, APIs, and specifications through the Model Context Protocol.

In this guide, I'll walk you through everything you need to configure **MCP servers in Gemini CLI**. From basic setup to advanced configurations with tools like **BrainGrid**.

## [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#what-is-a-gemini-cli-mcp-server) What is a Gemini CLI MCP Server?

A **Gemini CLI MCP server** is a bridge between Google's Gemini CLI and external services. MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives Gemini context beyond your local files. Think databases, APIs, cloud services, and project specifications.

When you connect a database MCP server to Gemini CLI, it can examine your actual tables and columns. The SQL it generates uses real schema names, not placeholders. When you connect **BrainGrid MCP**, Gemini reads your requirements and acceptance criteria directly, building features that match your specifications.

**What Gemini CLI MCP servers enable:**

- Query live database schemas
- Fetch real API responses
- Read structured specifications from BrainGrid
- Access GitHub issues, PRs, and commit history
- Connect to cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP)

Here's how the flow works:

```

External ServiceMCP ServerGemini CLIYouExternal ServiceMCP ServerGemini CLIYou"Show me REQ-142 from BrainGrid"Call get_requirement toolFetch requirement dataRequirement with acceptance criteriaStructured responseFull spec ready to implement
```

MCP transforms Gemini from a code generator into a context-aware development partner.

## [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#why-gemini-cli-mcp-servers-matter-for-developers) Why Gemini CLI MCP Servers Matter for Developers

Without MCP servers, every Gemini CLI session starts from scratch. You paste schemas, explain API structures, and fix the same boilerplate over and over. That copy-paste cycle kills momentum.

**With Gemini CLI MCP servers configured:**

- Database queries use your actual schema
- API code handles real response formats
- Specifications stay consistent across sessions
- Less manual fixing, faster shipping

The pattern applies across your entire stack. A GitHub MCP server gives Gemini context about open issues. A Stripe MCP server lets it understand billing flows. **BrainGrid MCP** provides structured requirements instead of vague prompts.

When Gemini has direct access to your systems, the code it generates works the first time.

## [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#how-to-set-up-gemini-cli-mcp-servers) How to Set Up Gemini CLI MCP Servers

Gemini CLI supports MCP server configuration through two methods. You can use CLI commands for quick setup, or JSON configuration files for persistent settings.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#adding-gemini-mcp-servers-via-cli) Adding Gemini MCP Servers via CLI

The `gemini mcp add` command configures MCP servers without editing files manually.

**Add a remote HTTP MCP server (like BrainGrid):**

```

1gemini mcp add --transport http braingrid https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp
```

**Add a remote SSE MCP server:**

```

1gemini mcp add --transport sse my-sse-server https://api.example.com/sse
```

**Add a local stdio MCP server:**

```

1gemini mcp add my-local-server python server.py -- --port 8080
```

The `--` separates Gemini CLI flags from arguments passed to the MCP server process.

**Add MCP server with environment variables:**

```

1gemini mcp add -e GITHUB_TOKEN=$GITHUB_TOKEN github npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github
```

**Add MCP server with custom headers:**

```

1gemini mcp add --transport http --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" my-api https://api.example.com/mcp
```

By default, Gemini CLI adds MCP servers to the project config (`.gemini/settings.json`). Use `-s user` to add to user config (`~/.gemini/settings.json`) instead.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#configuring-gemini-mcp-servers-in-settingsjson) Configuring Gemini MCP Servers in settings.json

For persistent Gemini CLI MCP configuration, edit your `settings.json` file directly.

**Gemini CLI MCP config file locations:**

- User config: `~/.gemini/settings.json`
- Project config: `.gemini/settings.json`

Here's an example `settings.json` with multiple MCP servers configured:

```

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "braingrid": {
4      "httpUrl": "https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp"
5    },
6    "github": {
7      "command": "npx",
8      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"],
9      "env": {
10        "GITHUB_TOKEN": "$GITHUB_TOKEN"
11      }
12    },
13    "postgres": {
14      "command": "npx",
15      "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres"],
16      "env": {
17        "DATABASE_URL": "$DATABASE_URL"
18      }
19    }
20  }
21}
```

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#gemini-cli-mcp-server-configuration-format) Gemini CLI MCP Server Configuration Format

Each MCP server entry uses specific properties that determine how Gemini CLI connects.

**Transport is determined by property name:**

- `httpUrl` for HTTP streaming transport (remote hosted MCP servers)
- `url` for SSE transport (Server-Sent Events MCP servers)
- `command` for Stdio transport (local subprocess MCP servers)

```

**Gemini CLI MCP configuration properties:**

| Property | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `httpUrl` | HTTP streaming endpoint URL for remote MCP servers |
| `url` | SSE endpoint URL for Server-Sent Events MCP servers |
| `command` | Executable path for local MCP servers |
| `args` | Arguments passed to the MCP server command |
| `env` | Environment variables (`$VAR` or `${VAR}` syntax) |
| `headers` | Custom HTTP headers for remote MCP servers |
| `cwd` | Working directory for local MCP servers |
| `timeout` | Request timeout in milliseconds (default: 600,000) |
| `trust` | Skip confirmation prompts when `true` |
| `includeTools` | Allowlist of MCP tool names to enable |
| `excludeTools` | Blocklist of MCP tool names to disable |

**Example Gemini MCP server with headers and timeout:**

```

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "authenticated-api": {
4      "httpUrl": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
5      "headers": {
6        "Authorization": "Bearer $API_TOKEN",
7        "X-Custom-Header": "value"
8      },
9      "timeout": 30000
10    }
11  }
12}
```

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#managing-gemini-cli-mcp-servers) Managing Gemini CLI MCP Servers

**List all configured MCP servers:**

```

1gemini mcp list
```

**Remove an MCP server:**

```

1gemini mcp remove braingrid
```

**Disable MCP server temporarily:**

```

1gemini mcp disable braingrid
2gemini mcp enable braingrid
```

**Check MCP server status inside Gemini CLI:**

```

1/mcp
```

This displays connection status, available tools, and any errors for each configured MCP server.

## [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#best-gemini-cli-mcp-servers-for-developers) Best Gemini CLI MCP Servers for Developers

Here are the MCP servers I find most useful with Gemini CLI:

- **Database MCP servers**: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, Supabase, Neon. Gemini queries schemas, understands relationships, and generates accurate SQL.

- **GitHub MCP server**: Read PRs, inspect issues, understand commit history. Repository context that influences code but doesn't live in local files.

- **Cloud platform MCP servers**: AWS, GCP, Heroku. Access deployment configs, logs, and environment-specific behavior.

- **Stripe MCP server**: Visibility into billing flows, subscriptions, webhooks. Debug payment logic with real context.

- **Playwright MCP server**: Browser automation and testing. Gemini runs and validates UI interactions.

## [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#troubleshooting-gemini-cli-mcp-server-issues) Troubleshooting Gemini CLI MCP Server Issues

**MCP server shows DISCONNECTED:**
Check the URL for typos. Test connectivity with `curl https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp`. VPNs and firewalls can block MCP traffic.

**OAuth popup doesn't appear:**
Gemini CLI MCP OAuth requires a local browser. It won't work in headless servers or SSH sessions. Authenticate on a machine with a browser, then copy `~/.gemini/mcp-oauth-tokens.json` to the target machine.

**MCP tools not showing up:**
Run `/mcp` to check connection status. Verify `includeTools` isn't filtering them out. Complete OAuth authorization if required.

**MCP server timeout errors:**
Increase the timeout in your Gemini CLI MCP configuration:

```

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "slow-server": {
4      "httpUrl": "https://api.example.com/mcp",
5      "timeout": 120000
6    }
7  }
8}
```

**Stdio MCP server won't start on Windows:**
Wrap commands with `cmd`:

```

1{
2  "mcpServers": {
3    "windows-server": {
4      "command": "cmd",
5      "args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "my-mcp-server"]
6    }
7  }
8}
```

**Changes not taking effect:**
Restart Gemini CLI after modifying `settings.json` or adding new MCP servers.

## [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#frequently-asked-questions-about-gemini-cli-mcp-servers) Frequently Asked Questions About Gemini CLI MCP Servers

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#what-is-a-gemini-cli-mcp-server) What is a Gemini CLI MCP server?

A Gemini CLI MCP server is a service that connects to Google's Gemini CLI through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It gives Gemini context beyond your local codebase. This includes databases, APIs, cloud services, specifications, and any external system relevant to your application.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#how-do-i-add-an-mcp-server-to-gemini-cli) How do I add an MCP server to Gemini CLI?

Use `gemini mcp add` for quick setup, or edit `settings.json` directly. For example: `gemini mcp add --transport http braingrid https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp`. User config lives at `~/.gemini/settings.json`, project config at `.gemini/settings.json`.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#where-is-the-gemini-cli-mcp-configuration-file-located) Where is the Gemini CLI MCP configuration file located?

Gemini CLI stores MCP configuration in two locations:

- User-level: `~/.gemini/settings.json`
- Project-level: `.gemini/settings.json` in your repository root

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#what-mcp-servers-work-with-gemini-cli) What MCP servers work with Gemini CLI?

Any MCP server using stdio (local), SSE, or HTTP streaming transport works with Gemini CLI. This includes database servers (PostgreSQL, MySQL), GitHub, cloud platforms (AWS, GCP), and specification tools like BrainGrid.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#how-do-i-connect-braingrid-mcp-to-gemini-cli) How do I connect BrainGrid MCP to Gemini CLI?

Run `gemini mcp add --transport http braingrid https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp` or add `{"braingrid": {"httpUrl": "https://mcp.braingrid.ai/mcp"}}` to your `mcpServers` config. Authorize via browser on first connection.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#how-does-gemini-cli-mcp-compare-to-cursor-or-claude-code-mcp) How does Gemini CLI MCP compare to Cursor or Claude Code MCP?

All three support the MCP standard. MCP servers work across all tools. For setup guides, see our [Claude Code MCP](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/claude-code-mcp), [Cursor MCP](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/cursor-mcp), and [Windsurf MCP](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/windsurf-mcp) guides. The main differences are configuration format and CLI commands.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#why-is-my-gemini-cli-mcp-server-not-connecting) Why is my Gemini CLI MCP server not connecting?

Run `/mcp` inside Gemini CLI to check connection status and error messages. Common issues include incorrect URLs, missing OAuth authorization, network restrictions, or timeout settings too low.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#does-gemini-cli-support-mcp-server-authentication) Does Gemini CLI support MCP server authentication?

Yes. Gemini CLI handles OAuth automatically for MCP servers that require it. It opens your browser for authorization and stores tokens at `~/.gemini/mcp-oauth-tokens.json`. API key authentication is supported via environment variables in your MCP server config.

### [\#](https://www.braingrid.ai/blog/gemini-mcp\#can-i-use-multiple-mcp-servers-in-gemini-cli) Can I use multiple MCP servers in Gemini CLI?

Yes. Add multiple entries to the `mcpServers` object in your `settings.json`. Gemini CLI connects to all configured MCP servers and makes their tools available in your session.

### [​](https://docs.augmentcode.com/context-services/mcp/quickstart-gemini-cli\#3-configure-the-mcp-server-in-gemini-cli)  3\. Configure the MCP server in Gemini CLI

Gemini CLI reads the MCP server configuration from a settings file. You can configure MCP servers at either the user level (applies to all projects) or project level (applies only to that specific project):**Configuration file locations:**

- **User settings**(global):

  - macOS/Linux: `~/.gemini/settings.json`
  - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.gemini\settings.json`
- **Project settings** (optional): `.gemini/settings.json` in your project’s root directory

Add the following configuration to your Gemini CLI settings file:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "augment-context-engine": {
      "command": "auggie",
      "args": ["--mcp", "--mcp-auto-workspace"]
    }
  }
}
```
